entries.title: US confirms it has weapons in space
entries.summary: The US Space Force justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China. Beijing responded by urging Washington to "stop preparing for war" in outer space.
entries.content:
Published September 15, 2026last updated September 15, 2026

The US Space Force justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China. Beijing responded by urging Washington to "stop preparing for war" in outer space.

The United States has weapons deployed in spatial orbit, the US Space Force said, confirming the existence of such capabilities for the first time.

"The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a US Space Force spokesperson said in a press release. The statement did not provide specifics on the weapons in question.

"Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain — employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," it said, adding that "these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes."

US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink also confirmed the existence of US weapons in space, while speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday.

The Space Force, the US military's arm dedicated to space, justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China. It said both countries pose a threat to American interests in space.

China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts," the statement read. 

What have China and Russia said?

In response, China urged Washington to "stop preparing for war" in outer space.

"We urge the US side to stop expanding its military capabilities and preparing for war in outer space," Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, warning against an "arms race" in space.

Russia on Tuesday also called for space to be kept free of weapons.

"We believe that space must be free of any weapon," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow, adding: "We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarization of space."

The final frontier

The militarization of space is an issue as old as the race to space itself.

In 1967, the world's biggest superpowers and other nations signed the Outer Space Treaty addressing the single biggest concern — the deployment of nuclear weapons in space.

Since then, Russia, the US, India and China have been exploring ways to fight in space outside of that treaty. That includes targeting each other's satellites critical for military communication, navigation and surveillance. 

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Lithuania
entries.summary: The drone, which is believed to have entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus, was shot down by an Italian fighter jet in between the cities of Vilnius and Kaunas. There have been no reports of casualties or damage.
entries.content:
Lithuania

NATO jets shoot down drone over Lithuania

Published September 15, 2026last updated September 15, 2026

The drone, which is believed to have entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus, was shot down by an Italian fighter jet in between the cities of Vilnius and Kaunas. There have been no reports of casualties or damage.

A drone which entered Lithuanian airspace in the early hours of Tuesday morning was shot down by NATO fighter jets in between the cities of Vilnius and Kaunas, Lithuanian authorities have confirmed.

Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center (NKVC) said the drone most likely came from neighboring Belarus, an ally of Russia in its ongoing war against Ukraine, and was flying west when it was shot down by an Italian jet.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda thanked the military alliance for its "swift response."

"With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region," he wrote on social media. "Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said the NATO response sent "a clear message that NATO stands vigilant, committed, and ready."

What do we know about the latest drone incident?

Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the NKVC, told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT that the drone most likely entered from Belarus and flew along the outskirts of populated areas for about 30 minutes before being intercepted.

The Lithuanian armed forces published video from the ​site of the crash near the village of Pratkunai, close to Lithuania's second-largest city, Kaunas, and about 80 kilometers (50 miles) west of the capital, Vilnius.

The footage showed debris scattered in grass. Some of the parts appeared to be made from wood ⁠and ​some appeared charred.

The commander of the Lithuanian air force, Antanas Matutis, said that the drone had "likely" been carrying explosives.

Lithuania: Was the drone from Russia or Ukraine?

Officials have not indicated whether the drone was Russian or Ukrainian.

While Russia has been launching almost daily drone and missile strikes against Ukraine since the start of its full-scale invasion over four years ago, Ukraine has also been responding with drone strikes of its own.

Ukrainian drones, which often pass close to Lithuanian, Latvian and Estonian airspace en route to targets in northwestern Russia, have occasionally been jammed by Russian defenses and steered off course into NATO airspace.

Fighter jets with the NATO ​Baltic Air Defense mission have patrolled the skies over Latvia, Lithuania and ​Estonia since the Baltic ‌countries joined the alliance in 2004. The mission's jets shot down stray Ukrainian drones over Estonia ​in May, ⁠and over Latvia in June and August.

The Lithuanian military said Tuesday's incident marked the first time that a drone had been shot down in its airspace.

How has NATO responded?

Tuesday's incident came less than 24 hours after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said that strikes "close to the alliance's territory" would drive the trans-Atlantic organization to increase its support for Ukraine.

"Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine," he said, adding that drone strikes and incursions near NATO territory showed Russian President Vladimir Putin's "desperation" and "desire to sow fear and terror."

On Tuesday, Poland, a NATO ally and neighbor of Lithuania, also announced "aviation operations" had commenced in its airspace "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory."

These actions are of a "preventive nature" and are aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions," said authorities in Warsaw.

Germany's armed forces, the Bundeswehr, are also currently building up a German armored brigade in Lithuania. The combat-ready and independently deployable force, comprising 4,800 troops, is expected to be operational by 2027.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Russian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter
entries.summary: Denmark has summoned Russia's ambassador over a Baltic Sea encounter that Copenhagen says is part of an increasingly aggressive pattern of Russian behavior.
entries.content:
Denmark

Russian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter

September 15, 2026

Denmark has summoned Russia's ambassador over a Baltic Sea encounter that Copenhagen says is part of an increasingly aggressive pattern of Russian behavior.

A Russian warship fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea, with one passing close to the aircraft, Denmark's armed forces said on Tuesday.

The confrontation comes amid heightened security concerns on NATO's eastern flank during Russia's war in Ukraine.

How has Denmark responded?

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident fitted a broader pattern of increasingly aggressive Russian behavior in Europe.

She accused Moscow of intensifying its "hybrid war against Europe" and testing and challenging NATO, and called on European countries to strengthen their defenses.

"Reckless action from Russia towards Danish military during a routine overflight yesterday. Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver," Frederiksen said in a statement on X.

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen condemned the incident as "completely unacceptable" and summoned Russia's ambassador, saying the action could have put lives at risk.

The foreign minister accused Moscow of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour," adding: "That is something we cannot accept."

What happened in the Baltic Sea?

Denmark's armed forces said one of its Fennec helicopters was carrying out a routine photographic reconnaissance mission when the incident occurred.

The helicopter was observing a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser, a Danish port on the Baltic Sea.

The Russian vessel fired two flares towards the helicopter, according to the Danish military.

"One of the flares passed at close range to the helicopter," it said. No one on board was injured.

The incident came against a backdrop of growing tensions along NATO's eastern flank. Poland has repeatedly scrambled fighter jets during Russian attacks on neighboring Ukraine and reported incursions by Russian drones into its airspace.

NATO members in the region have stepped up air patrols and other defenses as Moscow's war in Ukraine has increasingly raised fears of spillover and direct confrontations between Russian and alliance forces.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: China tightens travel rules over tech security
entries.summary: Beijing says the new rules, which could also apply to foreign and Taiwanese nationals, are aimed at safeguarding "national security."
entries.content:
China

China imposes new travel restrictions over tech security

September 15, 2026

Beijing says the new rules, which could also apply to foreign and Taiwanese nationals, are aimed at safeguarding "national security."

Sweeping travel restrictions on Chinese citizens came into effect on Tuesday, including exit bans for people considered to have endangered China's "industrial or technological security."

The new exit-and-entry rules, which were passed in July, apply to citizens deemed to have violated technology import and export regulations, particularly in the field of artificial intelligence.

The State Council in Beijing said the new rules were formulated to "safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."

The regulations apply not only to people within China but also to Chinese citizens deemed to have committed criminal acts abroad.

In such cases, citizens could be "prohibited from leaving the country for a period of six months to three years from the date of their return to China," said the State Council.

Travel bans give Beijing 'wide remit'

The restrictions come as China remains locked in a technological arms race with the United States, with both countries accusing each other of stealing locally developed AI models in recent months.

And analysts warn that the full scope of the new rules will only become clear once they start being implemented.

Security and criminal activities "can be vaguely defined and easily adjusted," said Chong Ja Ian, an analyst from the National University of Singapore, telling the AFP news agency that Beijing has given itself a "wide remit."

Will China's new travel bans affect foreigners?

Under the new regulations, foreign nationals could also be denied entry to China for up to five years if found to have made false statements in ​visa applications.

Foreign governments have often reported instances of citizens being denied permission to leave China due ⁠to security-related ​investigations.

Analyst Chong highlighted the recent case of US citizen Min Zin who the US government said was detained improperly in Yunnan province in June.

"The case of Min Zin is a reminder that the range of people [that Beijing] could restrict from exiting could be quite wide – and potentially arbitrary," he said.

Chinese travel bans: Taiwan warns citizens

The new rules could have particular implications for Taiwanese nationals who work in the tech sector and who travel between Taiwan and China.

Authorities in Taipei have warned citizens to take extra care on visits to China, which considers people from Taiwan to be Chinese citizens.

Beijing has dismissed any such concerns, claiming the rules provide better legal protection for Taiwanese.

Dylan Loh, an associate professor at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told AFP the travel restrictions "send a message" that China will take action to prevent "leaks in security or national interest-sensitive areas."

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Netherlands: Suspected sabotage disrupts train services
entries.summary: A major outage has hit parts of the Dutch railway system after objects were found placed across lines, authorities say. The company responsible for rail infrastructure says it suspects deliberate wrongdoing.
entries.content:
Netherlands

Netherlands: Suspected sabotage disrupts train services

September 15, 2026

A major outage has hit parts of the Dutch railway system after objects were found placed across lines, authorities say. The company responsible for rail infrastructure says it suspects deliberate wrongdoing.

Train services in various parts of the Netherlands have been severely disrupted, with ProRail, the company that maintains the nation's rail infrastructure, saying that sabotage was possibly at play.

National railway company NS said that train services around the central cities of Zwolle, Deventer and Amersfoort have been affected since the morning rush hour.

What do we know about the causes of the disruption?

In a statement, rail authority ProRail said that "[m]aterials deliberately placed on the tracks have been found at several locations. This is causing track-circuit failures. It appears to be a case of sabotage."

The ‌objects caused failures ‌across ​the network, affecting several level crossings, which disrupted ​road traffic, Pro Rail said.

ProRail ​workers ​were clearing the ​objects and ‌working to restore safe conditions, it ​added.

Though the company itself did not say what the "materials" were, a ProRail spokesperson told the daily de Volkskrant that "pipes had been found attached to the line" in several places.

This caused the disruptions, as the railway security systems can register a train's presence on a line because of an object placed on it and thus block access for other trains.

The spokesperson told the paper that one train had even collided with one of the pipes laid on the tracks, but that no accident or injuries had occurred.

Important event in The Hague

It remains unknown whether the incident has to do with so-called Prinsjesdag, the day the Dutch government presents its annual budget to parliament, where the reigning monarch gives a speech.

On the day, thousands of people go to The Hague to watch the royal family ride through the city in horse-drawn carriages.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: India: Meta to report child abuse cases to law enforcement
entries.summary: Tech giant Meta will now directly report child safety-related cases to India's cybercrime portal, according to media reports. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India: Meta to report child abuse cases to law enforcement

Published September 15, 2026last updated September 15, 2026

Tech giant Meta will now directly report child safety-related cases to India's cybercrime portal, according to media reports. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Amid intense scrutiny in India over alleged paid ads promoting child sexual abuse material, social media giant Meta will now reportedly lodge cases related to child safety with Indian law enforcement agencies
  • Air India's CEO has been summoned after three Italian nationals "skipped" immigration at Delhi airport and left the country

Here are the latest developments from India on Tuesday, September 15:

Skip next section Suspect arrested in viral Gurugram woman biker hit-and-run case

Suspect arrested in viral Gurugram woman biker hit-and-run case

The driver of a car accused of hitting a female motorbike rider in Gurugram — a satellite city of Delhi — was arrested on Tuesday, two days after a video of the incident went viral, triggering widespread outrage on social media.

Shivani Chauhan, who identifies herself as Sia, was riding with a group of her biker friends on Sunday when the incident took place.

In footage shot on a bike-mounted camera shared on Sia's Instagram profile, a white sedan is seen hitting her bike, sending her rolling over on the concrete road as her bike skids away.

The video has a voiceover of Sia in Hindi, wherein she alleges that the driver of the car was trying to "chase" her from the start and "fled" after hitting her.

The video shows the car driver gesturing towards Sia.

"He (the driver) told me to stop the bike, and trust me they all were drunk," the biker said, referring to the people in the car.

Sia said that her friend tried to flag the car down after she was hit.

The video purportedly shows the friend trying to open the car's door at a red light before the vehicle drives off.

The Gurugram police registered the case after the video quickly gained online traction.

What does the accused say?

The driver, identified as Kalyan Bainsla, was arrested in the state of Rajasthan on Tuesday.

The case was initially registered with charges of rash driving and endangering life or personal safety. Police then also added a charge of attempted murder, which carries a jail sentence of up to 10 years.

Bainsla, a gym owner, has denied hitting Sia deliberately. He also claims that he did not realize initially that a woman was among the group of bikers.

"I was traveling with my family. I didn't make any gestures at the young woman; I simply asked her to ride her bike slowly. I admit that a collision occurred. Had I stopped right then, those people would have beaten us up," he was quoted by Indian media as saying.

Speaking to ANI on Tuesday, Bainsla's lawyer accused the group of bikers, which he said had some 20-30 riders, of "speeding" and "performing stunts."

"The collision between the car and the bike occurred simply because of the speed at which they were driving. It is strictly a case of negligence — nothing more to it than that," lawyer Naveen Bainsla told ANI.

Skip next section Air India CEO summoned over alleged immigration lapse: reports

Air India CEO summoned over alleged immigration lapse: reports

The Indian government has summoned Air India's CEO over an alleged procedural lapse that saw three Italian nationals reportedly fly out of Delhi airport without undergoing a required departure immigration clearance, news agency ANI reported on Tuesday.

India's Ministry of Civil Aviation has reportedly issued a show-cause notice to Air India and has sought explanation on the alleged violation of immigration procedures.

On September 4, the Italian nationals flew into the Indian capital from the city of Amritsar. A short time later, they left Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport for Germany's Munich on board a Lufthansa flight without the mandatory immigration check, Indian media reports said.

Air India and Lufthansa have a codeshare partnership.

The Civil Aviation Ministry has deemed the incident a "serious security and immigration-related lapse," ANI reported, citing sources.

Skip next section Meta to report child sexual abuse material to India's cybercrime portal: reports

Meta to report child sexual abuse material to India's cybercrime portal: reports

Meta has agreed to report child safety-related matters, including child sexual abuse cases, to law enforcement agencies in India, Indian media reported on Tuesday, citing government sources.

News agency PTI quoted a Meta spokesperson as saying the cases would now be reported to the cybercrime portal managed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre.

The US tech giant has come under fire in India in recent months over alleged paid advertisements promoting AI-generated child sexual abuse material on its Facebook and Instagram platforms. 

"Meta has agreed to report child safety-related matters to the appropriate law enforcement agencies. It is a first step towards making the platforms safe for children and much more needs to be done," news agency ANI quoted unnamed government sources as saying.

The Indian government is engaging with other online platforms to ensure that they identify and remove such content proactively, news agency PTI cited government sources as saying.

ANI and PTI also quoted sources saying that the government would take action against platforms that fail to take proactive measures to ensure online child safety.

The news agencies were told by the sources that online safety of children is a "fundamental principle" for any social media platform operating in India and was "non-negotiable."

Meta under scrutiny in India

In July, an investigative report by the BBC found that Instagram had been running paid advertisements promoting child sexual abuse material in India.

India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) later ordered Instagram to disable all ads and content promoting and facilitating access to such material.

The ministry also demanded a detailed explanation on the issue and held several rounds of discussions with top Meta executives.

Last week, India's National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) summoned the managing director and head of Meta India over its inquiry into alleged ads related to child sexual exploitative and abuse material.

Meanwhile, a US-based nonprofit Tech Transparency Project (TTP) published a report saying that it had found more than 300 ads with child sexual abuse material that ran on Facebook and Instagram this year.

It said that 84 of the ads ran in India — 78 of them after the Indian government directive to Meta to remove any Instagram ads promoting child sexual abuse material.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our Tuesday news wrap of all the biggest headlines that are making a splash in India.

First up, Meta has reportedly agreed to flag child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as the US tech giant faces growing scrutiny in the South Asian nation over child safety.

In another development, the CEO of the country's flag carrier — Air India — has been summoned by the civil aviation ministry over an immigration lapse that saw three foreign nationals flying out of India without a mandatory departure immigration clearance.

Meanwhile, in news from the world of international relations, India and Vietnam are boosting their defense ties, including through co-production of military hardware

Stay tuned as we bring you all this and more.

entries.title: Why top AI researchers are warning about human extinction
entries.summary: Could artificial intelligence pose an existential threat to humanity? Some leading researchers are warning against an unregulated race toward AI superintelligence.
entries.content:
TechnologyGlobal issues

Why AI researchers warn of human extinction risks

September 15, 2026

Could artificial intelligence pose an existential threat to humanity? Some leading researchers are warning against an unregulated race toward AI superintelligence.

Dramatic warnings about the existential risks posed by artificial intelligence to humanity are nothing new.

As early as in the 1940s, the renowned scientist and science fiction author Isaac Asimov explored potential risks and unintended consequences of intelligent machines.

In 1991, Hollywood blockbuster "Terminator 2" imagined a dystopian 2029 in which an out-of-control military AI called Skynet directs killer robots in a war against humanity.

If the warnings of several of the biggest names in AI are to be believed, a similar scenario could become a reality — even before 2029.

Growing calls for strict regulation

"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," AI researcher Jacob Coxon posted on X last week, without exactly explaining how it might happen.

"No other human activity poses this level of danger," he added.

Coxon also revealed that he had quit his job at Anthropic, a US-based AI company, in protest against what he saw as an irresponsible race among AI companies to develop an ever better, self-improving superintelligence.

He warned that algorithms could begin to analyze and improve their own source code independently, which could shrink development cycles from several months to just a few minutes and thus make them uncontrollable.

Coxon is not an isolated voice. Nobel Prize-winning physicist Geoffrey Hinton, often called the "Godfather of AI," has been warning for years about the serious consequences of artificial superintelligence.

In 2023, he left his job at Google to publicly warn of the dangers of AI technologies he helped pioneer. Yoshua Bengio, a pioneer of artificial neural networks and deep learning, has also expressed concern about current developments and called for government regulation.

As recently as July 2026, more than 1,000 employees of leading AI companies warned in an open letter of an imminent loss of control if the race for "superintelligence" were not subject to significantly stricter regulations.

Caught in an unregulated race?

Despite the growing warnings, US President Donald Trump's administration has clearly shifted its AI policy toward minimizing regulatory hurdles and accelerating AI development.

In his X post, Jacob Coxon indirectly criticized the consequences of this policy: "At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes. At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk."

Coxon, who had moved from OpenAI to Anthropic in early 2026, is familiar with both corporate cultures.

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, he said that under the "most aggressive scenarios," things could spiral out of control as early as the end of 2027.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for his part, is currently calling for a coordinated, industry-wide slowdown in development to buy time to address the risks and prevent any misuse of AI.

In a lengthy essay shared on X over the weekend, he wrote that in six to 12 months, AI agents "could be capable ​of taking over the entire internet" and potentially cause "hundreds of billions of dollars in damage" without proper guardrails.

Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said they agree with Amodei.

The alignment problem

In recent years, numerous experts have voiced concern about the rapid AI advances, particularly the development of artificial general intelligence, which refers to systems that not only solve individual tasks but also match or exceed human intellectual capabilities in nearly all areas.

Sophisticated AI models, for instance, may pursue goals in ways that diverge from human intentions, something AI security researchers refer to as the "alignment problem."

On top of that, even developers can't always fully understand how AI makes certain decisions.

And so, it's no surprise that Coxon's former colleague Evan Hubinger came to his defense.

"Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger, who himself is the team lead for alignment stress tests at Anthropic, wrote on X.

In his post, Hubinger made clear that Anthropic hasn't yet found a solution to the alignment problem and warned that an AI model might begin to resist being shut down, because that would limit its ability to achieve its programmed goal.

Exaggerated hysteria?

Other AI experts, however, consider such doomsday scenarios to be extremely unlikely.

Among the most prominent critics of the so-called "AI doomers" is Meta's chief scientist, Yann LeCun. In October 2024, he dismissed such concerns as "complete nonsense."

Still other experts note that developing AI systems requires enormous amounts of computing power, energy, data and infrastructure.

They argue that an AI model cannot simply take over the world because it would need to rely on servers, power grids, communication systems and physical resources that are controlled by humans.

Does the real danger lie elsewhere?

In fact, many experts see the short-term risks not so much in the extinction of humanity as in the numerous indirect consequences of AI systems that already exist even without superintelligence.

These include disinformation campaigns on an unprecedented scale and the related manipulation of democratic processes, an expansion of mass surveillance, and job losses across numerous industries.

Just last week, Anthropic revealed that there had been several attempts by users to misuse its Claude AI models for research that could support biological weapons development. The company said it had banned the accounts involved.

In August, Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI caused a stir when they announced that their AI systems had unintentionally carried out autonomous hacking activities.

Following reports of further AI hacking attacks during testing, even top US AI frontier labs are now expressing a willingness to slow down the development of the technology.

This piece was originally published in German.

entries.title: El Salvador court hands down first life sentence for femicide
entries.summary: The landmark conviction comes 42 days after the killing of a woman in Santa Ana who prosecutors said was stalked and harassed by her neighbor.
entries.content:
El Salvador

El Salvador court hands down 1st life sentence for femicide

September 15, 2026

The landmark conviction comes 42 days after the killing of a woman in Santa Ana who prosecutors said was stalked and harassed by her neighbor.

A court in El Salvador has sentenced a 39-year-old man to life in prison for aggravated femicide, a statement from the prosecutor's office said.

It marks the first time in the country's history that a life sentence has been imposed for femicide. 

"Just 42 days after the crime, the Attorney General's Office of the Republic of El Salvador (FGR) obtained a life sentence for aggravated femicide," authorities announced in a post on X.

The defendant was found guilty of stabbing his neighbor to death in the western city of Santa Ana in August. According to prosecutors, Eduardo had been "constantly harassing the victim" before the attack.

The landmark conviction follows a number of recent legal reforms promoted by the country's right-wing president, Nayib Bukele.

Bukele's tough-on-crime policies

In April, El Salvador's legislature approved reforms allowing life imprisonment for severe crimes, including homicide, rape, femicide, and terrorism. Previously, the maximum prison sentence was 60 years, with the possibility of reductions for good behavior.

The reform is part of President Bukele's broader strategy to combat crime and insecurity. In 2023, Bukele inaugurated the Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), a mega-prison that has been widely criticized by human rights organizations.

Bukele governs under a state of emergency, and his war on gangs has led to the imprisonment of more than 90,000 people while significantly reducing crime and homicide rates. However, UN experts and NGOs have raised concerns about human rights violations, including crimes against humanity, amid the crackdown. 

A longstanding problem

El Salvador has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. In the 2010s, the rate of killings frequently exceeded  12 femicides per 100,000 women. In 2016 alone, more than 500 women were killed. 

According to feminist organizations, COVID-19 lockdowns worsened the situation by exposing more women to domestic violence and limiting access to support services.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Iran and America: A tale of two lands and the pistachio between them
entries.summary: The pistachios sold across the US have a surprising history: California's trees trace their roots to Iran. Now both regions face the same threat: their farmland is sinking as groundwater disappears.
entries.content:
September 15, 2026

The pistachios sold across the United States have a surprising history: California's trees trace their roots to Iran. Now both regions face the same threat: their farmland is sinking as groundwater disappears.

Hand-width cracks crisscross Armin's pistachio orchard in southeastern Iran, damaging irrigation pipes and swallowing precious water as the ground beneath him sinks.

"You look, and the earth has opened its mouth, and the water just pours in," Armin says. He has seen the cracks spread rapidly over the past five years, and worries his children may not be able to work the land as his father and grandfather did before him.

Armin, whose real name DW has chosen not to reveal for security reasons, lives in the arid region of Rafsanjan. For generations, farmers there have cultivated the pistachio tree for its small green edible seed used in everything from ice cream to the viral Dubai chocolate.

The region has long covered much of the world's demand for pistachios, but a combination of drought and groundwater extraction for irrigation has made Rafsanjan one of the fastest-sinking areas in Iran. One study found parts of the ground are dropping by up to 37 centimeters (14 inches) annually. And that is impacting production. 

It's a similar picture in California, where some pistachio farmers are also seeing their ground sink. Joe Coelho's family has cultivated the crop since 2000, and he says while his farm in Fresno is not directly affected, "growers are very aware of the risk."

Some areas nearby are facing serious water problems, says Coelho, who is the director of sustainability at American Pistachio Growers. "Subsidence is absolutely a serious issue in parts of the San Joaquin Valley."

The same pistachio and the same problems

The link between growers in the two countries goes back to the 1960s when US famers started building a pistachio industry. They did it using an Iranian variety — the pistachio that now dominates most Californian orchards is called Kerman, named after a city near Armin's farm.

California has recently overtaken Iran as the world's largest pistachio producer, with most of the crop grown in the Central Valley, where Coelho has his orchard. And though it is one of the world's most productive farming regions, there are places where the ground is sinking by as much as 20 centimeters a year.

Like in Iran, the problem is that more water is being pumped from underground aquifers for crop irrigation than is flowing back in.

"As surface water reliability has declined, growers have relied more heavily on groundwater," Coelho told DW, adding that he has witnessed the land change. "In certain areas, the soil does not have the same structure or water movement it once had."

Pistachio orchards in the Central Valley use around 4% of the valley's crop water. In Rafsanjan, more than nine in 10 liters of groundwater go to pistachio orchards.

As groundwater levels drop from overpumping, spaces within the aquifer collapse, and the earth above begins to sink in a process called land subsidence.

"Land subsidence in Iran is a man-made hazard, not a natural one like an earthquake," says Ali Beitollahi, who leads subsidence research at Iran's Road, Housing and Urban Development Research Center. "Much of the damage cannot be undone. When an aquifer collapses, it can never hold as much water again as before."

Older farmers in Rafsanjan remember reaching water at depths of just 20 meters (66 feet), says Armin. Today, many have to drill down to 300 meters. Some farmlands near Armin's are dead or dying, he says, while other orchards have been abandoned as wells dried up.

It's another blow to the struggling farmers, who says the boom driven by food trends like Dubai chocolate never reaches them because international sanctions and global competition have stripped Iran of the markets it once held as the world's biggest pistachio producer.

"We used to be known for quality," he says. "Now we are known for the low price."

Two pistachio regions, two different responses

The biggest difference between the two regions is how they are responding to the crisis. 

In California, the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), passed in 2014, requires water agencies to balance pumping and recharge in groundwater basins by 2040.

Managed aquifer recharge is one method the state is using to do so. It entails allowing water to recharge aquifers in rainy years, by flooding farmlands for instance, as a store for drought. Coelho is taking part in a pilot project that does just that.

SGMA has seen some progress. According to California's Department of Water Resources, groundwater levels have risen in four out of 10 monitored wells. But large parts of the Central Valley are still sinking.

Helen Dahlke, professor of integrated hydrologic sciences at the University of California, Davis, says recharge alone is not likely to offset decades of overexploitation of groundwater.

"Agriculture is by far the largest consumptive use of water in the Central Valley, so bringing groundwater basins into balance will likely require aligning crop water demand with the long-term water available under a warmer and more variable climate."

In Iran, awareness of groundwater management and subsidence has grown over the past decade among scientists but remains limited, says Ali Beitollahi. He worked on draft subsidence regulations that are currently awaiting government approval.

Pointing to the example of Japan's capital Tokyo where subsidence rates fell dramatically after authorities restricted groundwater pumping, he believes the problem could be managed if the state were to act quickly. Though given the current political situation in Iran, swift action is unlikely.

Another urgent step, he says, "is changing how farmers water their fields immediately, and teaching them why it matters."

Most of Rafsanjan's orchards are still flood-irrigated, meaning large amounts of water are lost to evaporation before it reaches plant roots.

Armin says he is trying to learn from US growers, but that many older farmers are set in their ways.

The meaning of a pistachio

Across California's Central Valley, the pressures of a warming climate, drought and diminishing groundwater are hard to ignore.

"We live with it every day," Coelho says, adding that California's pistachio farmers also need better water policy as well as better infrastructure and protection of water rights.

"Financial sustainability, water sustainability and environmental sustainability are connected," he told DW.

Armin doesn't see a future in pistachio farming. But when he looks at a single pistachio, he sees more than a crop competing for water or a snack on a shelf half a world away. He sees the history and the present of his family and his region.

"This pistachio sometimes comes from a tree 100 years old," he says. "It has paid for a wedding, for a child's education, for someone's happiness. Its money comes, and it creates a life."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Europe launches two climate observation satellites
entries.summary: The European Space Agency has put two satellites into orbit to take a closer look at the impact of climate change. One of them will focus particularly on plant life.
entries.content:
September 15, 2026

The European Space Agency has put two satellites into orbit to take a closer look at the impact of climate change. One of them will focus particularly on plant life.

Two satellites designed to enhance the monitoring of extreme weather events linked to climate change have been successfully sent into orbit by the European Space Agency (ESA).

The Vega-C rocket carrying the Sentinel-3C and Flex satellites lifted off from the Kourou space center in French Guiana at 10:21 p.m. Monday (0121 GMT Tuesday), with the two spacecraft entering sun-synchronous orbit within two hours of lift-off.

What will the Flex satellite do?

The Flex (Fluorescence Explorer) satellite aims to provide data on the impact of heat waves on plant matter by monitoring the very faint fluorescence emitted by plants when they carry out photosynthesis.

That fluorescence gives an indication of how efficiently vegetation is converting sunlight and carbon dioxide into energy.

The measurements provided by the satellite will thus "help scientists assess plant health, ecosystem productivity and the effects of environmental stress and climate change," according to ESA.

The €350 million ($403.5 million) mission is planned to last three years.

The satellite will orbit the Earth 14 times a day, revisiting particular locations every 27 days.

What is the role of the Sentinel-3C satellite?

The Sentinel-3C satellite is to collect data from the marine environment, including temperature, wave height and ocean currents.

It will also monitor land use and land cover with the aim of optimizing yields to prevent food crises.

Sentinel-3C is part of Copernicus, the Earth observation component of the EU’s space program.

Simonetta Cheli, the director of Earth Observation Programmes at the ESA, described the missions as "essential" in helping with the "climate change we are experiencing."

Edited by Richard Connor
